section_1.title: The Hook: An Unexpected Connection
section_1.content: Introduce the counter-intuitive puzzle: How can a series of elastic collisions between two blocks on a frictionless track result in the digits of Pi? Briefly demonstrate the phenomenon visually.
section_1.example: A tiny block (mass m) and a large block (mass M = 100^n * m) sliding on a track, where the number of collisions equals the first n digits of Pi.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
section_2.content: Establish the foundational rules: Conservation of Momentum and Kinetic Energy in 1D elastic collisions. Use a graphical velocity vector diagram to show how velocities swap or reverse during bounces.
section_2.example: A 2D scatter plot showing the 'velocity space'—where the state of the two blocks is a single point moving along an ellipse representing constant energy.

section_3.title: Mapping Collisions to Geometry
section_3.content: Explain the Galperin billiard-ball transformation. Show how the collision process can be unwrapped into a sequence of reflections of a ray within a circular wedge, effectively turning a 1D collision problem into a 2D geometric arc length problem.
section_3.example: Visual animation showing the 'phase space' trajectory bouncing off the circular arc of a unit circle sector.

section_4.title: The Limit of Mass Ratios
section_4.content: Explain why the mass ratio M/m = 100^n is critical. As the mass of the wall/large block becomes infinite, the angle of the 'bounce' in the phase space approach becomes smaller, approximating the circumference of a circle.
section_4.example: An animation of a 'Pac-Man' shaped wedge; as M/m increases, the reflection points trace out the arc length proportional to Pi.

section_5.title: Conclusion and Intuition
section_5.content: Summarize the 'Physics-to-Math' bridge: Pi emerges because collisions track the angle of a rotating vector in phase space. Encourage students to view complex series through the lens of geometric transformations.
section_5.example: A final visual summary: 1 collision = 3, 100 = 31, 10000 = 314. The blocks are essentially acting as a physical computer calculating digits.

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["Mass ratios dictate the wedge angle size.", "As mass grows, reflections trace an arc.", "The arc length corresponds to value Pi."]
        self.setup_layout("The Limit of Mass Ratios", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===

        axes = Axes(x_range=[0, 10, 2], y_range=[0, 3, 1], axis_config={"include_tip": False})

        self.play(Indicate(dot))
        self.play(FadeOut(dot))
